title: Business Continuity Management (BCM)
description: How BCM keeps critical business functions running in a disaster: its goals, the business impact assessment, BCP and DRP plans, testing and restoration order.

nodes.title: Focuses on critical and essential functions of business
nodes.description:
BCM does not try to cover every business process and system.
In a disaster you usually cannot keep the whole business running as usual. So decide which processes and systems matter most, and focus your limited resources on them.
BCM is the business process that drives planning and preparation for disasters:
1. Run the BIA (Business Impact Analysis).
2. Use its results, the measurements of time (RPO, RTO, WRT and MTD), to create BCPs (Business Continuity Plans) and DRPs (Disaster Recovery Plans).
3. Test the plans, train people on them, and maintain them.
The point is to keep the most important processes and systems running during a disaster, so that the business survives.

children.title: Goals of BCM
children.description: The three major goals of BCM, in priority order: first protect human life, then limit the harm the disaster causes, then make sure the organization lives on.

children.title: 1. Safety of people
children.description:
The number one, most important goal: protect human life.
Staff are the most valuable asset of an organization. Without them there is no organization.

children.title: 2. Minimize damage
children.description: The second goal: reduce, as far as possible, the impact and harm the disaster causes.

children.title: 3. Survival of business
children.description: The third goal: make sure the organization lives through the disaster and continues to operate.

children.title: Business Impact Assessment
children.description:
The first major process in BCM.
It identifies the critical processes and systems, gets the owners to approve the numbers, and produces the measurements of time (RPO, RTO, WRT and MTD) that drive the BCP and DRP.
It also decides the restoration order.

children.title: Identify Critical Processes & Systems
children.description: The first part of the BIA: consult stakeholders from across the organization to find out which business activities, and the technology supporting them, matter most.

children.title: Measurements of Time
children.description:
The major output of the BIA: four values, approved by the process or system owner.
Each one is expressed as a duration: seconds, minutes, hours, days.
On a timeline:
- RPO: the period before the disaster, from business as usual up to the disaster.
- RTO: from the disaster to recovery.
- WRT: from recovery back to business as usual.
- MTD: covers RTO plus WRT.

children.title: RPO
children.description:
How much data the organization is willing to lose in a disaster.
The maximum tolerable data loss, measured as time. If the server explodes, how much data can you lose? Examples: 5 seconds, 10 minutes, 3 hours or 2 days worth of data.
Full name: Recovery Point Objective.

children.title: RTO
children.description:
The maximum tolerable time to recover systems to a defined service level.
Usually, how long it takes to bring the backup systems online.
Full name: Recovery Time Objective.

children.title: WRT
children.description:
The maximum tolerable time to verify system and/or data integrity, as part of returning systems to normal operations.
Full name: Work Recovery Time.

children.title: MTD
children.description:
Also called MAD.
The maximum time a critical process or system can be disrupted before the consequences for the business become unacceptable.
The MTD is always greater than or equal to RTO + WRT.
Full name: Maximum Tolerable Downtime.

children.title: Owner approval of #s and associated costs
children.description:
The process or system owner must sign off on the RPO, RTO, WRT and MTD values, and on what it will cost to meet them.
The reason: the owner pays for the recovery strategies needed to achieve those values.

children.title: Types of Plans
children.description:
The two major kinds of plan BCM produces: one keeps critical business processes running, the other restores the technology behind them.
The measurements of time drive how they are written.

children.title: Business Continuity Plan (BCP)
children.description:
Focuses on critical business processes, and on the survival of the business.
Example: paying employees is usually a critical business process. If the automated payroll system blows up, the BCP covers how to keep paying employees.

children.title: Disaster Recovery Plan (DRP)
children.description:
Focuses on restoring critical technology, infrastructure and systems.
Example: if the payroll system explodes, the business may keep paying people by other means, while the DRP restores the actual payroll system.

children.title: Testing Plans
children.description:
BCPs and DRPs must be exercised periodically. A plan that was never tried out and refined is unlikely to work in a real disaster.
Exercises usually run in order: start with the simplest one, refine the plan based on the results, then move up to the next, more complete one, and so on.

children.title: Read-through / Checklist
children.description:
The first and simplest test.
The author of the plan reviews it alone to make sure nothing is missing, going through a checklist. Example: are the call tree names and alternate contact details correctly written in the plan?

children.title: Walkthrough
children.description:
An entirely paper-based exercise.
Stakeholders from across the business sit around a conference table with copies of the plan and go through it together step by step: page 1 says we do X, Y and Z.
The stakeholders are experts in their own areas (finance, customer relations, IT, business owners, etc.) and give feedback on the plan.

children.title: Simulation
children.description:
An entirely paper-based exercise, with stakeholders around a table with copies of the plan.
The key feature: you invent a scenario, such as a virus outbreak or an earthquake at a location, and everyone must follow the plan as if the disaster were happening.
You add updates or twists from time to time (this data center just went offline, CNN is on line 3) to see how well the plan works.

children.title: Parallel
children.description:
The first test that actually touches systems: only backup systems, NOT production systems.
Scenario-based: people react to an invented scenario using the plan, for example by bringing backup systems online.

children.title: Full-interruption / Full-scale
children.description:
The final and most important test: you actually cause a disaster.
Example: to find out if the backup power system works when the power is cut, cut the power.
Only do it after every other test has passed, and with management's approval.

children.title: Restoration order
children.description: How to decide which business processes and systems come back first after a disaster, and which follow: the most critical first, taking what each one relies on into account.

children.title: Most critical first
children.description:
Bring back the processes and systems the business can least do without before anything else.
Another important outcome of the BIA: business and system owners meet, argue it out, and decide which processes and systems truly matter most and in what sequence to bring them back.

children.title: Dependency charts
children.description:
A system usually cannot be brought up on its own. You must consider which other systems it needs, and bring those up first, in the right sequence.
Dependency charts map this out.
